en.title: Chemistry: the whole course
en.short: What chemistry covers, how chemistry degrees are organised, and how to study the subject well.

sections.heading: What chemistry is
sections.text:
Chemistry is the study of matter: what substances are made of, how their particles are arranged, how they change, and what energy is taken in or given out. It links physics, biology, medicine, engineering, agriculture and industry. A chemist may analyse water, design a drug, test a fuel or control a factory process.

The subject is both experimental and theoretical. Laboratory work teaches observation, measurement and safe handling. Theory explains why reactions happen and lets you predict products. Chemistry also has professional and ethical duties: protect people, the public and the environment.

These notes teach principles. They do not replace your laboratory manual, your institution’s safety rules, or the current regulations of your country. Follow local rules for chemicals, waste and emergencies.

sections.heading: How a degree is organised
sections.text:
Degrees and awards differ by country and institution, and they change. Check your own handbook for the current length, modules and rules.

In Nigeria, a BSc in chemistry commonly takes four years, and many programmes include an industrial attachment under SIWES, the Students Industrial Work Experience Scheme. Polytechnics commonly award ND and HND in science laboratory technology or related science programmes. In the UK, a BSc commonly takes three years in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and four in Scotland. Integrated master’s degrees such as MChem or MSci commonly add a year. Master’s degrees commonly take one to two years.

Most courses begin with shared science and mathematics, then move to core chemistry, laboratory work and a project. Later years allow options. A master’s adds advanced taught modules and a research dissertation. Professional bodies may accredit particular programmes; accreditation rules differ, so check the current list.

sections.heading: The main areas, in teaching order
sections.text:
Introductory topics start with measurement, units, significant figures and safe laboratory practice. Atomic structure and periodic trends follow, then chemical bonding and molecular shape. Stoichiometry and equations come next, with gases and kinetic theory, thermochemistry and enthalpy, solutions, concentration and colligative properties, chemical equilibrium, and acids, bases, pH and buffers. These give the language and quantitative tools for later work.

Core topics move into organic chemistry: structure and functional groups, stereochemistry and chirality, reaction mechanisms, carbonyl compounds and carboxylic acid derivatives, and aromatic chemistry. Inorganic core covers coordination chemistry and descriptive main-group and solid-state chemistry. Physical core covers chemical kinetics, thermodynamics (entropy and free energy), phase equilibria and electrochemistry. Analytical core covers volumetric and gravimetric analysis, then instrumental spectroscopy and chromatography. Applied core covers polymer chemistry, environmental and green chemistry, industrial chemistry and process principles, and chemistry ethics and professional practice.

Master’s level adds advanced organic synthesis and retrosynthesis, quantum chemistry and statistical mechanics, materials and nanochemistry, and research methods with a dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Learn the vocabulary first, but do not stop there. For every term, write a plain definition and one example. Use the periodic table often, and learn the common ions, formulas and functional groups until you can recall them.

Practice calculations by hand. Write the equation, convert to consistent units, show the cancellation, and check the answer for size and sign. In stoichiometry, identify the limiting reagent before calculating yield. In equilibrium and acid-base problems, write the reaction and the equilibrium expression before substituting numbers.

For organic chemistry, draw structures and mechanisms. Use curved arrows to show electron movement, and check formal charges. For analytical work, record raw data immediately and keep significant figures honest.

In the laboratory, read the risk assessment and safety data before the class. Know where the eyewash, shower, fire extinguisher and waste containers are. Never taste or smell a chemical directly. Ask when unsure. Study in short, regular sessions and test yourself without notes.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Mixing units is common: moles, grams, molarity, litres, joules and kelvin must be consistent. Ignoring significant figures gives false precision. Students also confuse moles with molarity, and mass with amount.

In equations, check that the equation is balanced and that states are shown where they matter. Do not confuse rate with equilibrium, or strong acids with concentrated acids. In acid-base work, check whether pH or pOH is asked for. In stoichiometry, check the limiting reagent.

In organic chemistry, arrows must start from an electron pair, not from an atom. Check stereochemistry and conditions. In the laboratory, never improvise with chemicals or waste. Record data as you go, not after the practical.

keyPoints: Chemistry studies the composition, structure, properties and changes of matter, and the energy involved.
Degree lengths and awards vary by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
Learn definitions, formulas and functional groups, then practise calculations and structures by hand.
Write units on every line, check significant figures, and ask whether an answer is reasonable.
In organic chemistry, use curved arrows to show electron movement and check formal charges.
Follow your institution’s safety rules and record laboratory data immediately.

en.title: Measurement, units and safe laboratory practice
en.short: SI units, significant figures, unit conversion, the mole and safe laboratory practice.

sections.heading: SI units and prefixes
sections.text:
The International System of Units (SI) has seven base units: metre for length, kilogram for mass, second for time, ampere for current, kelvin for temperature, mole for amount of substance, and candela for luminous intensity. Derived units combine these, such as newton = kg m/s².

Prefixes scale units by powers of ten: kilo (k) 10³, centi (c) 10⁻², milli (m) 10⁻³, micro (µ) 10⁻⁶, nano (n) 10⁻⁹. Write a space between number and unit, as in 25 mL and 0.50 mol.

sections.heading: Significant figures and uncertainty
sections.text:
Significant figures are the digits in a measurement that carry meaning. Non-zero digits count; zeros between them count; leading zeros do not; trailing zeros after a decimal point count. In multiplication and division, keep the least number of significant figures. In addition and subtraction, keep the least number of decimal places.

Every measurement has uncertainty. Absolute uncertainty has the same unit as the value. Relative uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ value, often given as a percentage. A result may be written 12.3 ± 0.1 mL.

sections.heading: Unit conversion and the mole
sections.text:
Convert units by multiplying by a factor equal to 1. Since 1 L = 1000 mL, 250 mL × (1 L ÷ 1000 mL) = 0.250 L.

The mole is the SI unit of amount. One mole contains the Avogadro number of entities, about 6.022 × 10²³. Molar mass M is the mass per mole in g/mol. Amount n = m ÷ M. Example: 9.0 g of water with M = 18.0 g/mol gives n = 9.0 ÷ 18.0 = 0.50 mol.

sections.heading: Safe laboratory practice
sections.text:
Wear safety goggles and a lab coat, and use gloves when needed. Read labels and safety data sheets (SDS), documents that describe a chemical’s hazards and how to handle it safely, before use. Never eat, drink or taste in the laboratory. Use a fume hood for volatile or toxic substances.

Heat test tubes at an angle, away from people. Carry glassware carefully and do not use cracked glass. Put waste in the correct container. Rules differ by institution and country, so follow your local training and supervisor.

keyPoints: SI has seven base units, and prefixes scale units by powers of ten.
In multiplication and division, keep the least number of significant figures; in addition and subtraction, keep the least decimal places.
Relative uncertainty = absolute uncertainty ÷ measured value.
Convert units by multiplying by a factor equal to 1, such as 1 L ÷ 1000 mL.
Amount in moles: n = m ÷ M, where M is molar mass in g/mol.
Wear goggles and a lab coat, read the safety data sheet, and follow your institution’s hazard and waste rules.

en.title: Atomic structure and periodic trends
en.short: Subatomic particles, atomic and mass numbers, isotopes, electron configuration and periodic trends.

sections.heading: Particles
sections.text: An atom has a small, dense nucleus of protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons. A proton has charge +1 and relative mass about 1; a neutron has charge 0 and relative mass about 1; an electron has charge −1 and relative mass about 1/1836. Atomic number Z is the number of protons and fixes the element. Mass number A is protons plus neutrons. Write A above Z before the symbol, as in ²³Na with Z = 11, meaning 11 protons and 12 neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons equal protons.

sections.heading: Isotopes
sections.text: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons, so same Z but different A. Their chemical behaviour is nearly identical, though masses differ. Relative atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average of isotope masses. Example: isotopes of mass number 10 and 11, with abundances 20% and 80%. Relative atomic mass ≈ 0.20 × 10 + 0.80 × 11 = 10.8. Divide percentage abundances by 100 before multiplying.

sections.heading: Electron configuration
sections.text: Electrons occupy orbitals in order of increasing energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, and so on. Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle). Within equal-energy orbitals, electrons occupy singly first (Hund’s rule). Sodium (Z = 11) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹; chlorine (Z = 17) is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. Outer-shell electrons are valence electrons and mainly control chemical behaviour.

sections.heading: Periodic trends
sections.text: Across a period, nuclear charge rises while shielding changes little, so effective nuclear charge (the net pull on outer electrons) increases. Atomic radius generally falls; ionisation energy and electronegativity generally rise. Down a group, outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and more shielded, so atomic radius rises and ionisation energy and electronegativity fall. Cations are smaller than their parent atoms; anions are larger. In an isoelectronic series (same electron number), the ion with more protons is smaller. Trends are general, with small irregularities.

keyPoints: Atomic number Z is the number of protons; mass number A is protons plus neutrons.
Isotopes have the same Z but different A, and relative atomic mass = Σ(isotope abundance fraction × isotope mass).
Electron configuration fills orbitals by increasing energy, following the Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule.
Across a period, atomic radius falls while ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the reverse occurs.
Cations are smaller than parent atoms and anions are larger; in an isoelectronic series more protons means smaller radius.
Effective nuclear charge is the net pull on outer electrons and explains the main periodic trends.

en.title: Chemical bonding and molecular shape
en.short: Ionic, covalent and metallic bonding, Lewis structures, VSEPR shapes, polarity and intermolecular forces.

sections.heading: Bond types
sections.text: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually after a metal transfers electrons to a non-metal. Ions form a lattice, so ionic solids are hard, have high melting points, and conduct only when molten or dissolved. Covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs between atoms; unequal sharing gives a polar covalent bond. Metallic bonding is a lattice of cations held by delocalised electrons, which explains conductivity and malleability.

sections.heading: Lewis structures
sections.text: A Lewis structure shows valence electrons as dots or lines for shared pairs. Count valence electrons, join atoms with single bonds, add lone pairs, and check the octet rule where it applies. Formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − half the bonding electrons; prefer formal charges near zero. Bond polarity arises from a difference in electronegativity, an atom’s pull on shared electrons; the bond is marked δ+ and δ− for its partial charges. Bond dipoles may cancel: CO2 is linear and nonpolar, while bent water is polar.

sections.heading: VSEPR shapes
sections.text: VSEPR means valence shell electron pair repulsion. Electron domains, bonding pairs and lone pairs, repel and stay as far apart as possible. Two domains give linear, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral. Lone pairs take more space than bonding pairs, so they reduce bond angles: CH4 is tetrahedral, NH3 trigonal pyramidal, H2O bent. Double and triple bonds count as one domain. The shape name describes atom positions, not lone pairs.

sections.heading: Intermolecular forces
sections.text: Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds. London dispersion forces act between all molecules and grow with more electrons and larger surface area. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules. A hydrogen bond is a strong dipole-dipole attraction when H is bonded to N, O or F and is attracted to a lone pair on another such atom. Ion-dipole forces act between ions and polar molecules. These forces affect boiling points, solubility and biological structure.

keyPoints: Ionic bonds are electrostatic attractions between ions; covalent bonds share electron pairs; metallic bonds use delocalised electrons.
In a Lewis structure, valence electrons are shown as dots or bond lines, and formal charge = valence electrons − nonbonding electrons − half the bonding electrons.
A bond is polar when electronegativity differs; a molecule is polar only if its bond dipoles do not cancel.
VSEPR arranges electron domains to minimise repulsion: two linear, three trigonal planar, four tetrahedral, with lone pairs reducing angles.
London dispersion, dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding and ion-dipole forces are weaker than covalent or ionic bonds but control physical properties.
Hydrogen bonds occur when H bonded to N, O or F is attracted to a lone pair on another N, O or F atom.

en.title: Stoichiometry and chemical equations
en.short: Balancing equations, mole ratios, limiting reagents and yield calculations.

sections.heading: Balancing equations
sections.text: Balancing means giving coefficients so every element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Change coefficients only, never subscripts. For CH4 + O2 -> CO2 + H2O, put 2 before O2 and 2 before H2O: CH4 + 2O2 -> CO2 + 2H2O. Check each element: carbon 1, hydrogen 4, oxygen 4 on both sides. An ionic equation must also balance charge.

sections.heading: Mole ratios
sections.text: The coefficients give the mole ratio. In 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, 2 mol H2 react with 1 mol O2 to form 2 mol H2O. Convert mass to moles using n = m ÷ M, where M is molar mass in g/mol. Then multiply by the ratio from the balanced equation. For gases at the same temperature and pressure, coefficients also give volume ratios.

sections.heading: Limiting reagent
sections.text: The limiting reagent is used up first and sets the maximum product. Divide the moles of each reactant by its coefficient; the smallest value is limiting. Example: 4.0 g H2 is 4.0 ÷ 2.0 = 2.0 mol. 16.0 g O2 is 16.0 ÷ 32.0 = 0.50 mol. For 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O, ratios are 2.0 ÷ 2 = 1.0 and 0.50 ÷ 1 = 0.50, so O2 is limiting. It forms 2 × 0.50 = 1.0 mol H2O, mass 1.0 × 18.0 = 18.0 g. This is the theoretical yield.

sections.heading: Yield calculations
sections.text: Actual yield is the mass obtained. Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%. If 15.0 g is collected, percentage yield = 15.0 ÷ 18.0 × 100% = 83.3%. Yield can fall below 100% through side reactions, incomplete reaction, losses in transfer or impure reactants. Values above 100% suggest wet or impure product, or an error. Always identify the limiting reagent before calculating yield.

keyPoints: Balance equations by changing coefficients, not subscripts, so atoms and charge balance.
The coefficients of a balanced equation give the mole ratio for reactants and products.
Convert mass to moles with n = m ÷ M, then use the mole ratio.
The limiting reagent is the reactant with the smallest moles ÷ coefficient; it sets the theoretical yield.
Theoretical yield is the maximum product mass from the limiting reagent.
Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100%.

en.title: Gases and kinetic molecular theory
en.short: Gas laws, ideal gas equation, partial pressures, kinetic theory and real gas behaviour.

sections.heading: The gas laws
sections.text: Boyle’s law says that at constant temperature the pressure of a fixed amount of gas is inversely proportional to its volume: P × V = constant. Charles’s law says that at constant pressure the volume is proportional to the absolute temperature in kelvin. Avogadro’s law says that equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules. Combining them gives PV ÷ T = constant for a fixed amount of gas. Convert Celsius to kelvin by adding 273.15.

sections.heading: Ideal gas equation
sections.text: For n moles, PV = nRT, where R is the gas constant, 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. This equation describes an ideal gas: point molecules with no forces between them except during collisions. Example: find the volume of 2.00 mol of gas at 300 K and 100 kPa. Use SI units: P = 100 000 Pa. V = nRT ÷ P = (2.00 × 8.314 × 300) ÷ 100 000 = 0.0499 m³, which is 49.9 dm³ (litres).

sections.heading: Partial pressures
sections.text: Dalton’s law of partial pressures states that in a mixture of non-reacting gases the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures: P_total = P₁ + P₂ + ... . The partial pressure of gas i is P_i = x_i P_total, where x_i is its mole fraction. This holds for ideal gases and is a good approximation for real gas mixtures at ordinary pressures.

sections.heading: Kinetic theory and real gases
sections.text: Kinetic theory explains the gas laws. It assumes gas molecules move randomly, collide elastically and have negligible volume. Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature. The root mean square speed is c_rms = √(3RT ÷ M), where M is the molar mass. Real gases deviate at high pressure and low temperature, where molecules are close and attractive forces matter. The van der Waals equation, (P + an² ÷ V²)(V − nb) = nRT, corrects for these: a for attraction, b for molecular volume.

keyPoints: Boyle’s law: PV = constant at constant temperature; Charles’s law: V ÷ T = constant at constant pressure.
The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT, with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
Dalton’s law: total pressure is the sum of partial pressures, and P_i = x_i P_total.
Kinetic theory gives c_rms = √(3RT ÷ M); average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature.
Real gases approach ideal behaviour at low pressure and high temperature.
The van der Waals equation is (P + an² ÷ V²)(V − nb) = nRT.

en.title: Thermochemistry and enthalpy
en.short: Heat, calorimetry, enthalpy changes, Hess law, standard enthalpies and bond energies.

sections.heading: Heat and calorimetry
sections.text:
Thermochemistry studies heat exchanged during changes. Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference. In calorimetry, a reaction heats or cools a known mass of water or solution, and q = mcΔT gives the heat gained or lost. Here m is mass, c is specific heat capacity (the energy needed to raise 1 g by 1 K) and ΔT is temperature change. For water, c is about 4.18 J g−1 K−1.

Example: 50.0 g of water rises by 10.0 °C, so q = 50.0 × 4.18 × 10.0 = 2090 J = 2.09 kJ. If 0.0500 mol of reaction caused this, the reaction released 2.09 kJ, so ΔH = −2.09 ÷ 0.0500 = −41.8 kJ mol−1.

sections.heading: Enthalpy changes
sections.text: Enthalpy H is a state function. At constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals the enthalpy change ΔH. Exothermic reactions release heat and have ΔH negative; endothermic reactions absorb heat and have ΔH positive. Thermochemical equations show the physical states and the value of ΔH, because changing state changes the energy.

sections.heading: Hess law
sections.text: Hess law says the total enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, not the route. So you can add known equations and their ΔH values to find an unknown one. Standard enthalpy changes are measured at a stated pressure, often 100 kPa, and often reported at 298 K. Standard enthalpy of formation is the change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states. Elements in their standard states have zero standard enthalpy of formation.

sections.heading: Bond energies
sections.text:
Bond dissociation energy is the energy needed to break one mole of a particular bond in the gas phase. Mean bond enthalpy is an average over similar compounds. For a gas-phase reaction, ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).

Example: H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl. Using approximate mean bond enthalpies H−H 436, Cl−Cl 243 and H−Cl 431 kJ mol−1: ΔH ≈ (436 + 243) − (2 × 431) = 679 − 862 = −183 kJ mol−1. The negative sign means the reaction is exothermic.

keyPoints: Heat exchanged is q = mcΔT, where c is specific heat capacity; for water c is about 4.18 J g−1 K−1.
At constant pressure, the heat exchanged equals ΔH; exothermic reactions have negative ΔH and endothermic reactions positive ΔH.
Hess law: the enthalpy change depends only on the initial and final states, so known equations and their ΔH values can be added.
Standard enthalpy of formation is for one mole of compound from elements in their standard states, and elements have zero.
For gas-phase reactions, ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
Mean bond enthalpies are averages, so bond-energy calculations give approximate ΔH values.

en.title: Solutions, concentration and colligative properties
en.short: Types of solution, solubility, concentration units, dilution and colligative properties.

sections.heading: Types and solubility
sections.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent. Solutions can be solid (brass), liquid (salt water) or gas (air). Solubility is the maximum amount that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a stated temperature. For solids in liquids it usually rises with temperature; for gases it falls as temperature rises and rises with pressure (Henry’s law). Like dissolves like: polar solvents dissolve ionic and polar solutes, non-polar solvents dissolve non-polar solutes. A saturated solution holds the maximum; an unsaturated one can dissolve more; a supersaturated one is unstable.

sections.heading: Concentration units
sections.text: Concentration expresses amount of solute per amount of solution or solvent. Molarity M = moles solute ÷ litres solution. Molality m = moles solute ÷ kilograms solvent. Mass percent = mass solute ÷ mass solution × 100. Mole fraction x = moles component ÷ total moles. Molarity changes with temperature because volume changes; molality does not. Example: 5.85 g NaCl (M = 58.44 g/mol) in 500 g water gives n = 5.85 ÷ 58.44 = 0.100 mol, so m = 0.100 ÷ 0.500 = 0.200 mol/kg.

sections.heading: Dilution
sections.text: Dilution adds solvent, so moles of solute stay constant: C1V1 = C2V2. Example: 25.0 mL of 0.200 M NaCl diluted to 100.0 mL gives C2 = 0.200 × 25.0 ÷ 100.0 = 0.0500 M. Always use the same volume units on both sides.

sections.heading: Colligative properties
sections.text: Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity, in dilute ideal solutions. They are vapour pressure lowering, boiling point elevation, freezing point depression and osmotic pressure. For a non-electrolyte: ΔTb = Kb m, ΔTf = Kf m, π = MRT. For electrolytes multiply by the van’t Hoff factor i, the number of particles per formula unit (ideal). Example: the 0.200 mol/kg NaCl above, with i = 2 and Kf = 1.86 °C kg/mol, gives ΔTf = 2 × 1.86 × 0.200 = 0.744 °C, so it freezes at about −0.744 °C.

keyPoints: Solubility is the maximum solute that dissolves at a stated temperature; gas solubility falls as temperature rises.
Molarity = moles solute ÷ litres solution; molality = moles solute ÷ kilograms solvent.
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2, because moles of solute do not change.
Colligative properties depend on particle number: ΔTb = Kb m, ΔTf = Kf m, π = MRT.
For electrolytes multiply colligative effects by the van’t Hoff factor i.
Use molality for boiling and freezing point calculations because it does not change with temperature.

en.title: Chemical equilibrium: reversible reactions and Le Chatelier
en.short: Reversible reactions, K and Q, Le Chatelier’s principle and simple equilibrium calculations.

sections.heading: Dynamic equilibrium
sections.text: Some reactions do not go to completion. In a reversible reaction, products react to give back reactants. When the forward and reverse rates become equal, the amounts stop changing. This is dynamic equilibrium: both reactions continue, but at equal rates. The system must be closed and at constant temperature. At equilibrium the concentrations are constant, not necessarily equal.

sections.heading: K and Q
sections.text: For a reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant is Kc = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ ([A]^a[B]^b), using equilibrium concentrations in mol/L. For gases, Kp uses partial pressures. Strictly, activities are used, so K has no units; many first-year texts use concentrations. K depends only on temperature for a given reaction. The reaction quotient Q has the same form but uses concentrations at any moment. If Q < K the forward reaction is favoured; if Q > K the reverse is favoured; if Q = K the system is at equilibrium.

sections.heading: Le Chatelier
sections.text: Le Chatelier’s principle: if a change disturbs an equilibrium, the system shifts in the direction that opposes the change. Adding a reactant shifts forward; removing a product shifts forward. Increasing pressure shifts toward the side with fewer gas molecules (if the numbers differ). Increasing temperature shifts in the endothermic direction and changes K. A catalyst speeds both directions equally and does not shift the position.

sections.heading: Worked calculation
sections.text:
Example: H2(g) + I2(g) ⇌ 2HI(g). At equilibrium in a 1 L vessel: [H2] = 0.20 M, [I2] = 0.20 M, [HI] = 1.60 M.
Kc = (1.60)² ÷ (0.20 × 0.20) = 2.56 ÷ 0.040 = 64.
If a mixture has [HI] = 0.80 M, [H2] = 0.40 M and [I2] = 0.40 M, then Q = 0.64 ÷ 0.16 = 4.0. Since Q < K, the forward reaction is favoured until Q reaches 64.
An ICE table lists initial, change and equilibrium amounts and helps organise the algebra.

keyPoints: A reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium when the forward and reverse rates are equal.
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, Kc = [C]^c[D]^d ÷ ([A]^a[B]^b).
Q has the same form as K but uses current concentrations; Q < K favours forward, Q > K favours reverse.
K changes with temperature, not with concentration or pressure alone.
Le Chatelier’s principle: a disturbance shifts equilibrium to oppose it; a catalyst does not shift it.
In the HI example, Kc = (1.60)² ÷ (0.20 × 0.20) = 64.

en.title: Acids, bases, pH and buffers
en.short: Acid and base definitions, strong and weak acids, pH and pOH, buffers and titration curves.

sections.heading: Acid-base definitions
sections.text: Arrhenius: acid gives H+ in water, base gives OH−. Brønsted-Lowry: acid donates a proton (H+), base accepts one; each has a conjugate partner. Lewis: acid accepts an electron pair, base donates one. Water is amphiprotic.

sections.heading: Strength and pH
sections.text:
Strong acids and bases ionise almost completely in water; weak ones ionise only partly and form an equilibrium. Ka measures acid strength, Kb base strength. For a weak acid, Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA]. pH = −log10[H+] and pOH = −log10[OH−]. At 25 °C, Kw = [H+][OH−] = 1.0 × 10^−14, so pH + pOH = 14.00; this changes with temperature.

Example: 0.010 M NaOH gives [OH−] = 0.010 M. pOH = −log10(0.010) = 2.00, so pH = 14.00 − 2.00 = 12.00 at 25 °C.

sections.heading: Buffer action
sections.text: A buffer resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added. It contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid. Added H+ is taken up by the base; added OH− is neutralised by the acid. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation estimates pH: pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]), where pKa = −log10 Ka. Capacity is greatest when [A−] is close to [HA], near pH = pKa. Example: pKa = 4.76 and [A−] ÷ [HA] = 1 gives pH = 4.76 + log10(1) = 4.76.

sections.heading: Titration curves
sections.text: An acid-base titration curve plots pH against volume of titrant added. A strong acid with a strong base gives a sharp jump near pH 7 at the equivalence point. A weak acid with a strong base starts higher, has a buffer region near pH = pKa, and its equivalence point is above 7. A strong acid with a weak base gives an equivalence point below 7. Indicators are chosen so their colour-change range lies on the steep part of the curve. The equivalence point is where moles of acid and base react completely; the end point is the observed colour change.

keyPoints: Brønsted-Lowry acids donate H+ and bases accept H+; Lewis acids accept electron pairs.
Strong acids and bases ionise almost completely; weak ones ionise only partly.
pH = −log10[H+] and pOH = −log10[OH−]; at 25 °C pH + pOH = 14.00.
For a weak acid, Ka = [H+][A−] ÷ [HA].
A buffer contains a weak acid and its conjugate base, or a weak base and its conjugate acid; pH = pKa + log10([A−] ÷ [HA]).
Titration curves show a sharp pH jump at the equivalence point; indicator choice depends on the steep region.

en.title: Organic structure and functional groups
en.short: Covers naming, drawing, isomerism, main functional groups and their effects on physical properties.

sections.heading: Naming and drawing
sections.text: An IUPAC name has a parent chain, a suffix for the principal functional group, and prefixes for substituents. Choose the longest carbon chain and number it to give the principal group the lowest locant. For example, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 is butan-2-ol: four carbons, an -ol suffix, and OH at carbon 2. A displayed formula shows every bond; a condensed formula groups atoms, as in CH3CH2OH; a skeletal formula shows the carbon skeleton and leaves C-H bonds understood.

sections.heading: Isomerism
sections.text: Isomers share a molecular formula but differ in structure. Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity: chain isomers (butane and 2-methylpropane), position isomers (propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol), and functional-group isomers (ethanol and dimethyl ether, both C2H6O). Stereoisomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement; they are covered in the stereochemistry summary. Each isomer has its own physical properties.

sections.heading: Functional groups
sections.text: A functional group is an atom or group that gives a molecule its characteristic properties. Main groups include alkene C=C, alkyne C≡C, haloalkane -X, alcohol -OH, ether -O-, amine -NH2, amide -CONH2, aldehyde -CHO, ketone -C(=O)-, carboxylic acid -COOH and ester -COOR. The principal group becomes a suffix, such as -ol, -al, -one, -oic acid, -amine or -amide; others are prefixes, such as hydroxy-, oxo-, amino- or chloro-. A homologous series has the same functional group and a regular CH2 difference.

sections.heading: Physical properties
sections.text: Functional groups control polarity and hydrogen bonding, which set boiling point and solubility. Alcohols and carboxylic acids donate and accept hydrogen bonds, so they boil higher and dissolve in water more than alkanes. Ethers can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate them; aldehydes and ketones are polar but do not donate hydrogen bonds. Amines can donate hydrogen bonds. A large hydrocarbon part is nonpolar and lowers water solubility. Amina compares ethane and ethanol: both have two carbons, but ethanol’s -OH hydrogen-bonds, so ethanol is a liquid and mixes with water; ethane is a gas and is not soluble.

keyPoints: IUPAC naming chooses the longest parent chain and the lowest locants for the principal functional group.
Displayed, condensed and skeletal formulas show different levels of structural detail.
Constitutional isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers differ only in spatial arrangement.
Functional groups such as -OH, -COOH, -NH2 and C=O control polarity and hydrogen bonding.
Hydrogen bonding raises boiling point and water solubility; a large hydrocarbon part lowers solubility.
A homologous series shares a functional group and differs by CH2.

en.title: Stereochemistry and chirality
en.short: Chirality, enantiomers, diastereomers, R/S and E/Z notation, optical activity and reaction stereochemistry.

sections.heading: Chirality and isomers
sections.text: A molecule is chiral if its mirror image cannot be superimposed on it. The common cause is a stereocentre: a carbon with four different groups. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images. They have identical physical properties except the direction they rotate plane-polarised light, and they react differently with chiral reagents. Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images; they differ in physical properties and can be separated. A meso compound has stereocentres but is achiral because it has an internal mirror plane.

sections.heading: R/S and E/Z
sections.text: Use the Cahn-Ingold-Prelog (CIP) rules. For a tetrahedral stereocentre, rank the four groups by atomic number, with higher atomic number first; duplicate atoms at a multiple bond. Point the lowest priority group away, then read 1 to 2 to 3: clockwise is R, anticlockwise is S. For an alkene, rank the two groups on each carbon. If the higher-priority groups are on opposite sides the configuration is E; if on the same side it is Z.

sections.heading: Optical activity
sections.text: Optical activity is the rotation of plane-polarised light by a chiral sample. Specific rotation is [α] = α ÷ (l × c), where α is observed rotation in degrees, l is path length in dm and c is concentration in g/mL. Example: 2.0 g in 50.0 mL gives c = 0.040 g/mL; with l = 2.0 dm and α = +5.2°, [α] = +5.2 ÷ (2.0 × 0.040) = +65°. A racemic mixture has equal enantiomers and zero rotation. Enantiomeric excess, ee = (observed rotation ÷ rotation of pure enantiomer) × 100%.

sections.heading: Reaction stereochemistry
sections.text: An SN2 reaction at a stereocentre proceeds with inversion of configuration. An SN1 reaction gives a planar carbocation and usually racemisation, often with some inversion. E2 elimination needs an anti-periplanar arrangement. Addition of bromine to an alkene is anti; hydrogenation on a metal surface is syn. Such outcomes are stereospecific when the mechanism fixes the configuration.

keyPoints: A chiral molecule is non-superimposable on its mirror image; a carbon with four different groups is a common stereocentre.
Enantiomers are mirror images with identical physical properties except optical rotation; diastereomers are not mirror images and differ in physical properties.
CIP: rank groups by atomic number, put the lowest away; clockwise is R, anticlockwise S. For alkenes, higher-priority groups opposite is E, same side is Z.
Specific rotation: [α] = α ÷ (l × c), with l in dm and c in g/mL.
Enantiomeric excess: ee = (observed rotation ÷ rotation of pure enantiomer) × 100%.
SN2 gives inversion, SN1 usually racemisation, E2 needs anti-periplanar, bromine addition is anti, hydrogenation is syn.

en.title: Organic reaction mechanisms
en.short: Curly arrows, substitution, elimination, addition, radicals, intermediates and pathway control.

sections.heading: Arrows and intermediates
sections.text: A curly arrow shows where an electron pair moves: tail on the source (bond or lone pair), head on the destination. Fishhook arrows show single-electron radical steps. A mechanism is a series of elementary steps through transition states, the highest-energy arrangements on the path. Intermediates are species formed and then consumed. A carbocation has a positive carbon, a carbanion a negative carbon, a radical an unpaired electron. Intermediates sit in shallow wells; transition states cannot be isolated. Rate depends on barrier height.

sections.heading: Substitution and elimination
sections.text: Nucleophilic substitution replaces a leaving group with a nucleophile, an electron-pair donor. SN2 is one concerted step: the nucleophile attacks the carbon opposite the leaving group as its bond breaks. It is favoured by primary substrates, strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents. SN1 goes through a carbocation, so tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents favour it. Elimination removes H and the leaving group to form C=C. E2 is concerted and favoured by strong or bulky bases and heat; E1 shares the carbocation route with SN1. Example: bromoethane with hydroxide gives ethanol mainly by SN2; 2-bromo-2-methylpropane with water gives substitution and elimination products through a carbocation.

sections.heading: Addition and radicals
sections.text: Electrophilic addition to an alkene starts with attack by an electrophile (an electron-pair acceptor), often H+, giving the more stable carbocation; the nucleophile then adds. Radical mechanisms have initiation (radicals formed), propagation (one radical consumed, another produced) and termination (radicals combine). Chlorination of methane: light splits Cl2 into Cl atoms, each Cl removes H from methane, and the methyl radical reacts with Cl2. Radical substitution is not selective, so mixtures form.

sections.heading: Pathway control
sections.text: Substrate structure, nucleophile or base strength, leaving-group ability, solvent, temperature and concentration decide the pathway. Good leaving groups are weak bases (I−, Br−, Cl−, sulfonate esters). Heat and strong base push elimination; strong nucleophile and primary substrate push SN2; polar protic solvent and tertiary substrate push SN1. Steric hindrance slows SN2 and encourages E2. Conditions can favour one product, but mixtures occur.

keyPoints: A curly arrow starts at an electron pair source and ends where that pair goes; fishhook arrows show single electrons.
SN2 is concerted and favoured by primary substrates, strong nucleophiles and polar aprotic solvents; SN1 goes through a carbocation and is favoured by tertiary substrates and polar protic solvents.
E2 is concerted and favoured by strong or bulky bases and heat; E1 shares the carbocation route with SN1.
Electrophilic addition to an alkene forms the more stable carbocation first; radical chains have initiation, propagation and termination.
Intermediates are real but short-lived species; transition states are energy maxima and cannot be isolated.
Substrate structure, reagent strength, leaving group, solvent and temperature decide whether substitution, elimination or addition dominates.

en.title: Carbonyl compounds and carboxylic acid derivatives
en.short: Aldehydes, ketones, acids, esters, amides and acid chlorides, with addition, substitution and condensation.

sections.heading: Carbonyl group
sections.text:
The carbonyl group is C=O. In an aldehyde, at least one atom bonded to the carbonyl carbon is hydrogen; in a ketone, the carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups. The polar C=O bond leaves the carbon electron-poor, so nucleophiles attack there. Aldehydes are usually more reactive than ketones because they are less hindered and have fewer electron-donating alkyl groups.

Carboxylic acids contain COOH. The OH makes them acidic and lets them form hydrogen bonds. Esters are RCOOR′, amides are RCONH2 or RCONR2, and acid chlorides are RCOCl. Here R and R′ are carbon groups.

sections.heading: Acids and derivatives
sections.text:
These compounds share an acyl group, RCO−, attached to a leaving group. Acid chlorides are the most reactive derivatives; amides are the least. Esters lie between. Hydrolysis converts them back to the acid: acid chlorides react vigorously with water, esters need acid or base and heat, and amides need stronger conditions. Acid chlorides also react with alcohols to give esters and with amines to give amides.

Example: CH3COCl + C2H5OH gives CH3COOC2H5 + HCl. Ethanoyl chloride plus ethanol gives ethyl ethanoate plus hydrogen chloride.

sections.heading: Nucleophilic addition
sections.text: Nucleophilic addition is characteristic of aldehydes and ketones. A nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, the π electrons move to oxygen, and a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate forms. Protonation then gives an alcohol. With HCN, propanone gives a cyanohydrin, C(CH3)2(OH)CN. Cyanide is toxic and must be handled safely.

sections.heading: Acyl substitution and condensation
sections.text:
In acyl substitution, a nucleophile attacks the acyl carbon, a tetrahedral intermediate forms, and the leaving group departs as the C=O bond returns. This is how acid chlorides become acids, esters or amides.

Condensation joins two molecules with loss of a small molecule. Fischer esterification is a condensation: carboxylic acid plus alcohol, with acid catalyst, gives ester plus water. Aldol condensation starts with an aldehyde or ketone that has an α-hydrogen; the aldol product can lose water to give an α,β-unsaturated carbonyl. Claisen condensation joins two esters in base to give a β-keto ester.

keyPoints: The carbonyl group is C=O; aldehydes have H on the carbonyl carbon and ketones have two carbon groups.
Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
Acid chlorides are the most reactive acyl derivatives and amides the least.
Nucleophilic addition to C=O gives a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, which is protonated to an alcohol.
Acyl substitution replaces the leaving group of an acid derivative and is how acid chlorides form acids, esters and amides.
Condensation joins two molecules with loss of a small molecule, as in Fischer esterification and aldol condensation.

en.title: Aromatic chemistry
en.short: Benzene and aromaticity, Hückel’s rule, electrophilic aromatic substitution and substituent directing effects.

sections.heading: Benzene and aromaticity
sections.text: Aromaticity is the extra stability of a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated molecule with a continuous ring of p orbitals. Benzene, C6H6, is the standard example: six carbon atoms in a regular hexagon, each contributing one p electron. Its six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, so benzene is drawn with a circle or two Kekulé structures. This delocalisation gives resonance energy, and benzene undergoes substitution rather than addition to keep the ring intact.

sections.heading: Hückel rule
sections.text: Hückel’s rule states that a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated system is aromatic if it has 4n + 2 π electrons, where n = 0, 1, 2, ... It is antiaromatic if it has 4n π electrons and can stay planar. If the ring is not planar or conjugation is broken, it is nonaromatic. Benzene has 6 = 4(1) + 2. Cyclobutadiene has 4 = 4(1) and is antiaromatic. Cyclooctatetraene has 8 = 4(2) but adopts a tub shape, so it is nonaromatic.

sections.heading: Electrophilic substitution
sections.text: Electrophilic aromatic substitution replaces a ring hydrogen. The electrophile attacks the π cloud to form a resonance-stabilised arenium ion, or sigma complex. Loss of a proton restores aromaticity. Common reactions are nitration with nitric and sulfuric acids, halogenation with a Lewis acid such as FeBr3, Friedel-Crafts alkylation or acylation with AlCl3, and sulfonation with sulfur trioxide. The product is still aromatic, so it can undergo further substitution.

sections.heading: Directing effects
sections.text: Substituents already on the ring control where the next group goes. Activating groups donate electron density and usually direct ortho and para. Examples are alkyl groups and groups with a lone pair on the atom attached to the ring, such as OH, OR and NH2. They stabilise the arenium ion, especially when the positive charge reaches the substituted carbon. Deactivating groups withdraw electron density and usually direct meta; examples are NO2, CN, SO3H and carbonyl groups. Halogens are deactivating but ortho and para directing because their lone pair still stabilises the intermediate by resonance.

keyPoints: Aromaticity requires a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring with 4n + 2 π electrons.
Benzene has six delocalised π electrons and gains resonance energy.
Electrophilic aromatic substitution proceeds through an arenium ion and restores aromaticity by losing a proton.
Activating groups such as OH, OR, NH2 and alkyl are ortho and para directing.
Deactivating groups such as NO2, CN, SO3H and carbonyl are meta directing.
Halogens are deactivating but ortho and para directing.

en.title: Coordination chemistry
en.short: Complexes, ligands, naming, isomerism, crystal field theory, colour and magnetism.

sections.heading: Complexes and ligands
sections.text: A coordination complex is a central metal ion bonded to ligands, ions or molecules that donate electron pairs. Coordination number is the number of donor atoms attached to the metal, not the number of ligands. Common values are 6 (octahedral) and 4 (tetrahedral or square planar). A monodentate ligand uses one donor atom, a bidentate ligand two, and a polydentate ligand several. Bidentate and polydentate ligands can form rings called chelates, often more stable than monodentate analogues.

sections.heading: Nomenclature and isomerism
sections.text: In names, the cation is named first, then the anion. Ligands are listed alphabetically, with prefixes di, tri, tetra for repeated ligands, and the metal oxidation state is given in Roman numerals in brackets. Example: [Co(NH3)4Cl2]Cl is tetraamminedichloridocobalt(III) chloride. Isomerism includes structural types (ionisation, hydrate, linkage, coordination) and stereoisomerism (cis/trans geometric and optical isomers). Linkage isomerism arises when an ambidentate ligand binds through different donor atoms.

sections.heading: Crystal field theory
sections.text: Crystal field theory treats ligands as point charges that split the metal d orbitals. In an octahedral field the lower t2g set lies below the upper eg set by Δo. In a tetrahedral field the splitting Δt is smaller, about 4/9 Δo. Electrons fill lower orbitals first; if Δo is large they pair in t2g (low spin), and if small they occupy eg before pairing (high spin). Whether high or low spin wins depends on Δo versus the pairing energy P.

sections.heading: Colour and magnetism
sections.text: Colour arises when an electron absorbs visible light and moves to a higher d level; the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed colour. Energy gap Δ = hν = hc/λ. Magnetic behaviour depends on unpaired electrons: diamagnetic complexes have none, paramagnetic complexes have some. The spin-only moment is μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. Example: high-spin d6 [Fe(H2O)6]2+ has n = 4, so μ = √(4×6) = √24 ≈ 4.90 BM; low-spin d6 [Fe(CN)6]4− has n = 0 and is diamagnetic.

keyPoints: Coordination number counts donor atoms bonded to the metal, not ligands.
IUPAC names list ligands alphabetically and give the metal oxidation state in Roman numerals.
Crystal field theory splits d orbitals; octahedral splitting is Δo and tetrahedral splitting is about 4/9 Δo.
Large Δo favours low spin and small Δo favours high spin, depending on the pairing energy.
Colour comes from d-d absorption; the observed colour is complementary to the absorbed light.
Spin-only magnetic moment is μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.

en.title: Descriptive inorganic chemistry: main group and solid state
en.short: Main group trends, key compounds, simple ionic solids, defects and structure-property links.

sections.heading: Main group trends
sections.text: Across a period, effective nuclear charge rises, so atomic radius falls and ionisation energy and electronegativity rise. Down a group, radius rises and ionisation energy falls. The inert pair effect makes heavier p-block elements prefer oxidation states two below the group maximum, as in Pb(II) and Bi(III). Diagonal relationships arise between similar charge-to-size ratios, such as Li and Mg. Important compounds include basic oxides of metals, acidic oxides of non-metals, hydrolysing chlorides such as SiCl4, and hydrides ranging from ionic to covalent.

sections.heading: Simple solids
sections.text:
A crystal structure is described by its unit cell, the repeating box, and by coordination number, the number of nearest neighbours of an ion. Close packing gives high density. Common ionic structures are rock salt NaCl (6:6), caesium chloride CsCl (8:8), zinc blende ZnS (4:4) and fluorite CaF2 (8:4). Radius ratio rules predict coordination only roughly; covalency and temperature also matter.

Example: NaCl has four formula units per face-centred cubic cell and a = 564 pm. Density ρ = ZM ÷ (N_A a³). M = 58.44 g/mol, N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
a³ = (5.64 × 10⁻⁸ cm)³ = 1.794 × 10⁻²² cm³
ρ = 4 × 58.44 ÷ (6.022 × 10²³ × 1.794 × 10⁻²²) = 2.16 g/cm³

sections.heading: Defects and properties
sections.text: Real crystals contain point defects. A Schottky defect is a missing cation and anion pair; a Frenkel defect is an ion moved from its lattice site to an interstitial site. Both raise entropy; Schottky defects lower density. Non-stoichiometric solids have variable composition, often through mixed oxidation states. Defects control ionic conductivity, colour centres and diffusion. Structure controls properties: diamond and graphite are both carbon but differ in hardness and conductivity because of bonding and packing. Polymorphs of the same compound can have different densities and reactivities.

keyPoints: Across a period atomic radius falls while ionisation energy and electronegativity rise; down a group the reverse occurs.
The inert pair effect favours lower oxidation states for heavier p-block elements.
Common ionic structures are rock salt 6:6, CsCl 8:8, zinc blende 4:4 and fluorite 8:4.
Unit-cell density is ρ = ZM ÷ (N_A a³), with a in cm for g/cm³.
Schottky defects are missing cation-anion pairs; Frenkel defects are displaced ions.
Defects and polymorphs change density, conductivity, colour and reactivity.

en.title: Chemical kinetics: rates, mechanisms and catalysis
en.short: Rate laws, integrated rate equations, half-life, Arrhenius equation, mechanisms and catalysis.

sections.heading: Rate laws and order
sections.text:
Reaction rate is the change in concentration per unit time, usually mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. For aA + bB → products, the empirical rate law is rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. The powers m and n are the orders in A and B; overall order is m + n.

They come from experiment, often initial rates, not from the balanced equation. The rate constant k depends on temperature and catalyst.

sections.heading: Integrated rates and half-life
sections.text:
For first order A → products, rate = k[A]. Integration gives ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt, so [A] = [A]₀e^(−kt). Half-life is t½ = ln2/k = 0.693/k, independent of concentration. Zero order gives [A] = [A]₀ − kt and t½ = [A]₀/(2k). One-reactant second order gives 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt and t½ = 1/(k[A]₀).

Example: k = 0.0693 s⁻¹ for a first-order reaction. t½ = 0.693 ÷ 0.0693 = 10.0 s. After 30.0 s, [A]/[A]₀ = e^(−0.0693 × 30.0) = e^(−2.079) = 0.125, so 12.5% remains.

sections.heading: Arrhenius and mechanisms
sections.text:
Arrhenius: k = A e^(−Ea/RT), or ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT). Ea is activation energy, A the pre-exponential factor, R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, T in kelvin. A plot of ln k against 1/T has slope −Ea/R.

A mechanism is a sequence of elementary steps summing to the overall reaction. Molecularity is the number of species in an elementary step. The slowest step is often rate-determining. For reactive intermediates, the steady-state approximation sets their net rate of change to zero; a fast pre-equilibrium step uses an equilibrium constant. The mechanism must give the observed rate law.

sections.heading: Catalysis
sections.text:
A catalyst raises rate by offering a lower-activation-energy pathway. It is not used up overall and does not change the equilibrium constant or reaction thermodynamics.

A homogeneous catalyst is in the same phase as reactants; a heterogeneous catalyst is in a different phase, often a solid surface. Enzymes are biological catalysts. Surface area and poisoning matter in industrial heterogeneous catalysis.

keyPoints: Rate law: rate = k[A]^m[B]^n; orders m and n are experimental, not stoichiometric.
First order: ln[A] = ln[A]₀ − kt and t½ = 0.693/k.
Zero order: [A] = [A]₀ − kt; second order: 1/[A] = 1/[A]₀ + kt.
Arrhenius: k = A e^(−Ea/RT), so ln k = ln A − Ea/(RT).
The rate-determining step controls the overall rate; intermediates need steady-state or pre-equilibrium treatment.
A catalyst lowers Ea and speeds the reaction without changing equilibrium or being consumed overall.

en.title: Chemical thermodynamics: entropy and free energy
en.short: The second and third laws, entropy changes, Gibbs and Helmholtz free energy, and equilibrium.

sections.heading: Entropy and the second law
sections.text:
Entropy S is a state function measuring how energy is dispersed among the accessible microstates; S = k ln W, where k is the Boltzmann constant and W the number of microstates. Units are J/K.

The second law states that for any spontaneous process the total entropy of the universe increases: ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0, with equality at equilibrium. For a system exchanging heat with surroundings at constant temperature T and pressure, ΔS_surroundings = −ΔH_system/T.

sections.heading: Third law and entropy changes
sections.text:
The third law says the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at 0 K. This lets us assign absolute standard molar entropies S° (J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), unlike enthalpies of formation.

For a reaction, ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants). Entropy increases with temperature, volume and number of particles, and for phase changes solid → liquid → gas.

sections.heading: Gibbs and Helmholtz free energy
sections.text:
The Gibbs free energy is G = H − TS. At constant temperature and pressure, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A process is spontaneous if ΔG < 0, nonspontaneous if ΔG > 0, and at equilibrium ΔG = 0.

The Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS plays the same role at constant T and volume. Because ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, the sign of ΔG can change with temperature; the crossover is at T = ΔH/ΔS.

sections.heading: Free energy and equilibrium
sections.text:
For a reaction under any conditions, ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, where Q is the reaction quotient. At equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0, so ΔG° = −RT ln K.

Example: if ΔH° = −50.0 kJ and ΔS° = −0.100 kJ/K, then at 298 K ΔG° = −50.0 − 298(−0.100) = −20.2 kJ, so K = exp(20,200 ÷ (8.314 × 298)) ≈ 3.5 × 10³. At 500 K, ΔG° = 0.

keyPoints: The second law requires ΔS_universe = ΔS_system + ΔS_surroundings ≥ 0 for a spontaneous process, with equality at equilibrium.
The third law sets S = 0 for a perfect crystal at 0 K, so standard molar entropies S° are absolute.
For a reaction, ΔS° = ΣS°(products) − ΣS°(reactants).
The Gibbs free energy is G = H − TS; at constant T and p, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, and ΔG < 0 means the process is spontaneous.
The Helmholtz free energy A = U − TS applies at constant T and V.
ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q, and at equilibrium ΔG° = −RT ln K.

en.title: Phase equilibria
en.short: Phase rule, one- and two-component diagrams, vapour pressure, distillation and phase-change thermodynamics.

sections.heading: The phase rule
sections.text: A phase is a distinct physical part of a system. A component is an independent chemical species. The Gibbs phase rule is F = C − P + 2, where F is the number of intensive variables that can change without changing the phases. For water (C = 1) at the triple point, P = 3, so F = 0. At liquid-vapour equilibrium, P = 2, so F = 1. At constant pressure, F = C − P + 1.

sections.heading: One-component diagrams
sections.text:
A P-T phase diagram shows which phase is stable. The triple point is where three phases coexist; the critical point is where liquid and gas become identical. Vapour pressure is the pressure of vapour in equilibrium with liquid or solid. At equilibrium the chemical potential μ is equal in every phase; for a pure phase change ΔG = 0, so ΔS = ΔH/T. The Clapeyron equation gives a boundary slope: dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV). Vaporisation has ΔV > 0, so the slope is positive; water melting has ΔV < 0, so its curve slopes backwards. The integrated Clausius-Clapeyron equation, with ideal vapour and constant ΔHvap, is ln(P2/P1) = −ΔHvap/R (1/T2 − 1/T1).
Example: water, ΔHvap = 40.7 kJ/mol, P1 = 101.3 kPa at T1 = 373 K. At T2 = 363 K:
ln(P2/P1) = −(40,700 ÷ 8.314) × (1/363 − 1/373) = −0.3615
so P2 ≈ 0.6966 × 101.3 = 70.6 kPa.

sections.heading: Two components and distillation
sections.text: For an ideal two-component liquid, Raoult’s law gives pA = xA P°A and pB = xB P°B, where P° is the vapour pressure of the pure liquid. Total pressure is pA + pB, and vapour mole fraction is yA = pA/P. A temperature-composition diagram shows bubble and dew points; the lever rule gives the amounts of each phase. Relative volatility α = P°A/P°B measures ease of separation. Simple distillation cannot separate an azeotrope, a mixture whose vapour has the same composition as the liquid. Ethanol-water is a minimum-boiling azeotrope; nitric acid-water is a maximum-boiling azeotrope.

keyPoints: Gibbs phase rule: F = C − P + 2; at constant pressure use F = C − P + 1.
At the triple point of a one-component system F = 0; at liquid-vapour equilibrium F = 1.
The Clapeyron equation is dP/dT = ΔH/(TΔV).
The Clausius-Clapeyron equation is ln(P2/P1) = −ΔHvap/R (1/T2 − 1/T1).
At phase equilibrium the chemical potential μ is equal in every phase and ΔG = 0, so ΔS = ΔH/T.
Raoult’s law and relative volatility α = P°A/P°B govern ideal distillation, and azeotropes cannot be separated by simple distillation.

en.title: Electrochemistry: cells, potentials and corrosion
en.short: Redox, galvanic and electrolytic cells, electrode potentials, the Nernst equation, batteries and corrosion.

sections.heading: Redox and cells
sections.text:
Redox means reduction and oxidation together. Oxidation is loss of electrons; reduction is gain.

In every cell the anode is where oxidation occurs and the cathode is where reduction occurs. A galvanic (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to produce electrical work. An electrolytic cell uses an external voltage to drive a non-spontaneous reaction. In a galvanic cell the anode is negative; in an electrolytic cell the anode is positive. The Daniell cell uses Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ and Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.

sections.heading: Electrode potentials
sections.text:
A standard electrode potential E° is a half-cell potential measured against the standard hydrogen electrode, whose E° is 0 V. Standard conditions are usually 298 K, 1 bar and unit activity.

Tabulated values are reduction potentials. For a cell, E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. A positive E°cell means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions. For the Daniell cell, E° = +0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V.

sections.heading: Nernst equation
sections.text:
The Nernst equation adjusts a cell potential for non-standard concentrations: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, where n is electrons transferred, Q is the reaction quotient and F is the Faraday constant, 96485 C/mol. At 298 K, E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q.

For Zn|Zn²⁺(0.10 M)||Cu²⁺(1.0 M)|Cu, n = 2 and Q = 0.10 ÷ 1.0 = 0.10. E = 1.10 − (0.0592 ÷ 2) log 0.10 = 1.10 + 0.0296 = 1.13 V. Concentrations approximate activities.

sections.heading: Batteries and corrosion
sections.text:
A battery is one or more galvanic cells. A primary battery is not rechargeable; a secondary battery is rechargeable. In a lead-acid battery the anode is lead, the cathode is lead(IV) oxide and the electrolyte is sulfuric acid. Its discharge reaction is Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O.

Iron corrosion is electrochemical: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ at an anodic site, while oxygen is reduced at a cathodic site. Rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide. Coating and sacrificial anodes such as zinc or magnesium slow corrosion.

keyPoints: Oxidation is loss of electrons and occurs at the anode; reduction is gain and occurs at the cathode.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; a positive value means the reaction is spontaneous under standard conditions.
Nernst equation: E = E° − (RT/nF) ln Q, or at 298 K E = E° − (0.0592/n) log Q.
Galvanic cells convert chemical energy to electrical work; electrolytic cells use external voltage to drive non-spontaneous reactions.
Primary batteries are not rechargeable; secondary batteries such as lead-acid are rechargeable.
Iron corrosion is electrochemical; sacrificial anodes such as zinc or magnesium protect steel.

en.title: Analytical chemistry: volumetric and gravimetric analysis
en.short: Sampling and errors, main titration types, gravimetric analysis and glassware calibration.

sections.heading: Sampling and errors
sections.text: An analysis is only as good as its sample. Sampling must be random and representative; a grab sample from one spot may not represent a bulk lot. Errors are systematic (bias, for example a miscalibrated pipette) or random (uncontrolled variation). Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is agreement between repeats. Report results with units, uncertainty and the method used. Blanks and certified reference materials help check bias.

sections.heading: Acid-base and redox
sections.text: In a titration, a standard solution of known concentration is added from a burette until the equivalence point. Acid-base titrations use a pH indicator or pH meter. For a monoprotic acid with a monobasic base such as NaOH, c_acid V_acid = c_base V_base at equivalence. Example: 25.00 cm³ of HCl needs 20.00 cm³ of 0.1000 mol/dm³ NaOH. c(HCl) = (0.1000 × 20.00) ÷ 25.00 = 0.0800 mol/dm³. Redox titrations use electron transfer, for example permanganate, which is self-indicating; the reaction stoichiometry must be balanced.

sections.heading: Complexometric and precipitation
sections.text: Complexometric titrations form a metal-ligand complex. EDTA is a common titrant for metal ions; it binds many metals in a 1:1 ratio, so moles of EDTA equal moles of metal. A buffer and a metal indicator such as murexide are used. Precipitation titrations form a sparingly soluble salt, for example chloride with silver nitrate (argentometry), and need careful indicator choice.

sections.heading: Gravimetric and calibration
sections.text: Gravimetric analysis converts the analyte into a pure, weighable solid. The mass of the solid is related to the analyte by stoichiometry. Example: chloride in a sample is precipitated as AgCl. If 0.2500 g sample gives 0.4000 g AgCl (M = 143.32 g/mol), moles AgCl = 0.4000 ÷ 143.32 = 0.002791 mol, so mass Cl (35.45 g/mol) = 0.09894 g, and percentage = (0.09894 ÷ 0.2500) × 100 = 39.58%. Glassware is calibrated by weighing the water it holds or delivers at a known temperature and correcting for water density; volumetric flasks and pipettes should be checked before accurate work.

keyPoints: Systematic error affects accuracy; random error affects precision.
For a 1:1 acid-base titration at equivalence (monoprotic acid with a monobasic base), c_acid × V_acid = c_base × V_base.
Redox titration calculations must use the balanced electron-transfer stoichiometry.
EDTA commonly forms 1:1 complexes with metal ions in complexometric titrations.
Gravimetric percentage = (mass of analyte ÷ mass of sample) × 100.
Calibrate glassware by weighing the water it holds or delivers; volume = mass ÷ density at the measured temperature.

en.title: Instrumental analysis: spectroscopy and chromatography
en.short: UV-visible, infrared, NMR and mass spectra, atomic spectroscopy, and gas and liquid chromatography.

sections.heading: Electronic and atomic spectra
sections.text:
UV-visible spectroscopy measures absorption of ultraviolet and visible light, which excites electrons between molecular orbitals. The Beer-Lambert law is A = εcl, where A is absorbance, ε is molar absorptivity, c is concentration and l is path length. Absorbance is logarithmic: A = log10(I0/I).

Example: ε = 12,000 L mol−1 cm−1, c = 2.5 × 10−5 mol/L and l = 1 cm give A = 12,000 × 2.5 × 10−5 × 1 = 0.30. Atomic spectroscopy uses free atoms in a flame or plasma. Atomic absorption measures light absorbed by ground-state atoms; atomic emission measures light emitted by excited atoms. Calibration curves convert signal to concentration.

sections.heading: Infrared and NMR
sections.text:
Infrared (IR) spectroscopy measures absorption of infrared radiation by molecular vibrations. Bonds absorb at characteristic wavenumbers, so IR identifies functional groups. Wavenumber is 1 ÷ wavelength.

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) places nuclei such as ¹H in a strong magnetic field and applies radiofrequency pulses. The chemical shift depends on the electron environment; splitting reveals neighbouring protons. NMR gives connectivity and stereochemistry.

sections.heading: Mass spectrometry
sections.text: Mass spectrometry ionises molecules, separates the ions by mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) and detects them. The molecular ion gives molecular mass; fragment ions give structural clues. High-resolution instruments give exact mass and hence molecular formula. A mass spectrum is a plot of ion abundance against m/z.

sections.heading: Chromatography
sections.text:
Chromatography separates components between a mobile phase and a stationary phase. Separation depends on repeated partition or adsorption. In gas chromatography (GC), the mobile phase is a gas and the stationary phase is a liquid or solid; it suits volatile, thermally stable compounds. In liquid chromatography (LC), the mobile phase is a liquid; reversed-phase LC uses a non-polar stationary phase and a polar mobile phase.

Retention time helps identify a peak under fixed conditions, and resolution depends on selectivity, efficiency and retention. Quantitation uses peak area with calibration.

keyPoints: Beer-Lambert law: A = εcl, and A = log10(I0/I).
IR absorption at characteristic wavenumbers identifies functional groups.
NMR chemical shift and splitting reveal electronic environment and neighbouring protons.
Mass spectrometry separates ions by m/z; the molecular ion gives molecular mass and fragments give structure.
Atomic absorption uses ground-state atoms, while atomic emission uses excited atoms.
Chromatography separates by partition or adsorption between mobile and stationary phases; retention time and peak area support identification and quantitation.

en.title: Polymer chemistry: synthesis, molecular weight and properties
en.short: Addition and condensation polymerisation, molecular weight averages, crystallinity and structure-property links.

sections.heading: Making polymers
sections.text: Addition polymerisation joins unsaturated monomers, usually alkenes, without losing a small molecule. An initiator starts a chain that grows by adding one monomer at a time. Polyethylene and polystyrene form this way. Condensation polymerisation is step-growth: monomers with two reactive groups join, often releasing water or HCl. Polyesters and polyamides (nylons) are examples. Step-growth builds molecular weight slowly, so high conversion is needed. Some step-growth polymers, such as polyurethanes, form without a small molecule; the defining feature is stepwise growth, not elimination.

sections.heading: Molecular weight
sections.text:
Synthetic polymers contain chains of different lengths, so averages are used. The number-average Mn = ΣNiMi ÷ ΣNi counts each chain equally. The weight-average Mw = ΣNiMi² ÷ ΣNiMi gives heavier chains more influence. Their ratio, Mw ÷ Mn, is the dispersity, or PDI. It is at least 1 and rises as the distribution broadens.

Example: equal numbers of chains of 10,000 and 20,000 g/mol.
Mn = (10,000 + 20,000) ÷ 2 = 15,000 g/mol.
Mw = (10,000² + 20,000²) ÷ (10,000 + 20,000) = 16,667 g/mol.
PDI = 16,667 ÷ 15,000 = 1.11.

sections.heading: Structure and crystallinity
sections.text: Polymer chains may be linear, branched or crosslinked. Their arrangement controls crystallinity, the fraction of the polymer packed into ordered regions. Regular, linear chains with small side groups crystallise readily. Atactic chains (random side-group orientation), branches, crosslinks and bulky side groups hinder packing and lower crystallinity. Crystallites melt at Tm; amorphous regions soften at the glass transition temperature Tg. Both rise with stronger chain interactions; Tm also rises with crystallinity.

sections.heading: Properties from structure
sections.text: Crystallinity usually raises stiffness, strength, density and melting point, but lowers transparency and toughness. Without crosslinks, chains slide on heating, giving thermoplastics that can be remelted. Crosslinks stop chains sliding, giving rigid thermosets or rubbery elasticity. Higher molecular weight improves strength and toughness but raises melt viscosity. Plasticisers sit between chains, lower Tg and make a polymer softer. So polyethylene can be a soft film or a stiff bottle, depending on branching and crystallinity.

keyPoints: Addition polymerisation is chain growth from unsaturated monomers; condensation polymerisation is step-growth and often releases a small molecule.
Mn = ΣNiMi ÷ ΣNi and Mw = ΣNiMi² ÷ ΣNiMi; dispersity PDI = Mw ÷ Mn is at least 1.
Regular linear chains crystallise more readily; branching, atacticity and crosslinks reduce crystallinity.
Crystallinity raises stiffness, strength, density and melting point but usually lowers transparency and toughness.
Crosslinks prevent chain flow, giving thermosets or rubber elasticity; plasticisers lower Tg.
Higher molecular weight improves strength and toughness but increases melt viscosity.

en.title: Environmental and green chemistry
en.short: Air and water pollutants, persistence, green chemistry principles and waste reduction.

sections.heading: Air pollutants
sections.text: Air pollutants are substances in air at harmful concentrations. Primary pollutants are emitted directly: sulfur dioxide from sulfur-containing fuel, nitrogen oxides from high-temperature combustion, carbon monoxide from incomplete combustion, and particulate matter (PM). Secondary pollutants form in air; tropospheric ozone forms when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds react in sunlight. PM and ozone harm lungs; sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides acidify rain. Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas that drives climate change.

sections.heading: Water pollutants and fate
sections.text: Water pollutants include nutrients (nitrate, phosphate), heavy metals such as lead and mercury, pesticides, solvents, pharmaceuticals, microplastics and pathogens. Excess nutrients cause eutrophication: algal growth, decay, oxygen depletion and fish kills. Persistence is how long a substance remains in the environment. A useful measure is half-life, the time for half the amount to disappear. For first-order loss, t1/2 = ln2 ÷ k. Example: k = 0.0693 day⁻¹ gives t1/2 = 0.693 ÷ 0.0693 = 10 days. Persistent, fat-soluble substances can bioaccumulate in organisms and biomagnify along food chains.

sections.heading: Green chemistry principles
sections.text: Green chemistry designs products and processes to reduce hazardous substances and waste. The twelve principles of Anastas and Warner include waste prevention, atom economy, less hazardous synthesis, safer solvents, energy efficiency, renewable feedstocks, catalysis, design for degradation and inherently safer chemistry. Atom economy = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100%. If 100 g and 80 g of reactants give 120 g of product, atom economy = 120 ÷ 180 × 100% = 66.7%; the rest is waste unless reused.

sections.heading: Waste and sustainable practice
sections.text: Waste reduction follows the hierarchy: prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover energy, then dispose. In the laboratory, use smaller scale, less hazardous solvents, separate waste streams and avoid unnecessary derivatives. Sustainable practice also uses life cycle assessment (LCA), which estimates impacts from extraction to disposal. Catalysis and process intensification lower energy and material use. Green chemistry does not mean zero risk; it means lower hazard and better resource efficiency, checked by measurement.

keyPoints: Primary pollutants are emitted directly; secondary pollutants form in the atmosphere, such as tropospheric ozone from nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds.
Major water pollutants include nutrients, heavy metals, pesticides, solvents, pharmaceuticals, microplastics and pathogens; excess nutrients cause eutrophication.
Persistence is measured by half-life; for first-order loss, t1/2 = ln2 ÷ k.
Persistent fat-soluble substances can bioaccumulate and biomagnify.
Green chemistry applies principles such as waste prevention, atom economy, safer solvents, catalysis and design for degradation.
Atom economy = mass of desired product ÷ total mass of reactants × 100%; waste reduction follows prevent, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, dispose.

en.title: Industrial chemistry and process principles
en.short: Feedstocks, unit operations, catalysts, reaction conditions, process economics and plant safety.

sections.heading: Feedstocks and routes
sections.text: A feedstock is the raw material a plant converts into products. Bulk plants start from cheap, abundant materials such as petroleum fractions, natural gas, coal, minerals, air or biomass. The route depends on feedstock price and purity, energy, catalyst, scale and local supply. Ammonia is made from hydrogen and nitrogen; hydrogen often comes from natural gas by steam reforming, but other routes exist. Country and year change which route is cheapest, so check prices and local supply.

sections.heading: Unit operations and conditions
sections.text: Unit operations are physical steps: distillation, absorption, extraction, filtration, heat exchange and drying. Unit processes are the chemical reactions. Reaction conditions, meaning temperature, pressure, concentration and residence time (average time in the reactor), are set to balance rate, equilibrium conversion, selectivity and catalyst life. A higher temperature may raise rate but lower equilibrium yield or damage the catalyst. The reactor and separation train are designed together because recycling unreacted material improves overall yield.

sections.heading: Catalysts
sections.text: A catalyst speeds a reaction by providing a lower-energy path; it does not change the equilibrium position. Heterogeneous catalysts are solids used with gas or liquid reactants; homogeneous catalysts are in the same phase. Key properties are activity, selectivity and stability. Selectivity is the fraction of converted reactant that becomes the wanted product. It reduces unwanted by-products. Catalysts deactivate by fouling, poisoning or sintering and may be regenerated. Catalyst cost and lifetime belong in the process economics.

sections.heading: Economics and safety
sections.text: Process economics compares capital cost (plant and equipment) with operating cost (feedstock, energy, labour, maintenance, waste). Yield, selectivity and atom economy (desired product mass ÷ total product mass) reduce waste. Example: to make 1,000 kg of product at 80% yield, theoretical product = 1,000 ÷ 0.80 = 1,250 kg. If stoichiometric feedstock need is 1.5 kg per kg theoretical product, feedstock = 1,250 × 1.5 = 1,875 kg. Safety uses inherent safety (removing hazards by design), HAZOP (hazard and operability study), safety data sheets, relief systems and interlocks. Legal duties vary by country; check the regulator.

keyPoints: Feedstock choice depends on cost, purity, availability, energy and local supply, and it changes with country and year.
Unit operations are physical separations; unit processes are chemical reactions.
Reaction conditions balance rate, equilibrium conversion, selectivity and catalyst life.
A catalyst lowers activation energy and raises rate but does not shift equilibrium.
Yield = actual product ÷ theoretical product × 100%, and recycling unreacted material can raise overall yield.
Process economics compares capital and operating costs; safety uses inherent safety, HAZOP, safety data sheets and relief systems, with legal duties varying by country.

en.title: Chemistry ethics and professional practice
en.short: Research integrity, safety duties, chemical regulation and responsible waste handling for chemists.

sections.heading: Research integrity
sections.text:
Research integrity means honesty and rigour from the first measurement to the published paper. Its core offences are fabrication (inventing data), falsification (changing or omitting data) and plagiarism (using another person’s words or ideas without credit).

Good practice includes keeping raw records, reporting methods and uncertainty fully, giving authorship only for real contribution, and declaring conflicts of interest. Chemistry results can affect medicines, food and safety rules, so a small dishonest number can cause real harm.

sections.heading: Safety as duty
sections.text:
Safety is an ethical duty, not only a set of rules. A risk assessment identifies each hazard, who may be harmed, the controls needed and whether they work.

Safety data sheets (SDS) and Globally Harmonised System (GHS) labels give hazard and handling information. You should refuse unsafe work, report near misses and never leave a hazard for the next person. The duty extends to cleaners, visitors and the public.

sections.heading: Regulation and waste
sections.text:
Chemical regulation sets legal duties for manufacture, storage, use and disposal. Rules differ by country, so check your national law and your institution’s current rules. The GHS provides a common system for classifying and labelling hazards.

Waste follows a hierarchy: avoid, reduce, reuse, recycle, recover, then dispose. Hazardous waste must be segregated, labelled, stored safely and sent to a licensed contractor. Never pour solvents or heavy-metal solutions down the drain.

sections.heading: Professional conduct
sections.text:
Professional responsibilities include competence, honesty, confidentiality and putting public safety before convenience or profit.

Case: Amina, a final-year student in a Nigerian university laboratory, is asked to relabel an expired solvent bottle with a new date. She should refuse, record the request, and report it to the safety officer. Expired solvents may form peroxides or change composition. Reporting protects the group and is the professional response.

keyPoints: Research integrity rests on honesty, complete records and fair authorship; fabrication, falsification and plagiarism are serious misconduct.
Safety is an ethical duty to colleagues, visitors and the public, supported by risk assessment, SDS and GHS labels.
Chemical regulation is national law, so check the current rules of your country and institution.
