Hazardous waste must be segregated, labelled, stored and disposed of through licensed routes, never down the drain.
A practising chemist must stay competent, declare conflicts and put public safety before convenience.
Speaking up about unsafe or dishonest practice is part of professional responsibility.

en.title: Advanced organic synthesis and retrosynthesis
en.short: Retrosynthetic analysis, protecting groups, chemoselectivity and planning multi-step organic syntheses.

sections.heading: Retrosynthetic analysis
sections.text: Retrosynthesis plans a synthesis backwards. The target is simplified by disconnections, imaginary bond breaks that suggest precursors. Each fragment is a synthon, an idealised piece; the real chemical used is its synthetic equivalent. Functional group interconversion (FGI) changes one group into another to reach a known reaction. Good disconnections use available starting materials, avoid unnecessary steps and keep stereochemistry in view. A retron is a structural pattern that suggests a known transform, a reverse reaction step. The plan is a hypothesis, tested forward in the laboratory.

sections.heading: Protecting groups
sections.text: A protecting group temporarily masks a reactive functional group so that reaction occurs elsewhere. It must be easy to add, stable under the planned steps, and removable without damaging the product. Orthogonal groups are removed by different, independent conditions. Acetals protect aldehydes and ketones; silyl ethers protect alcohols and are removed by fluoride; Boc protects amines and is removed by acid; Fmoc is removed by base, so Boc and Fmoc are orthogonal. Protecting groups add steps, so use them only when chemoselectivity fails.

sections.heading: Chemoselectivity
sections.text: Chemoselectivity is the preferential reaction of one functional group while others remain unchanged. It differs from regioselectivity, which chooses a site in the molecule, and stereoselectivity, which chooses a stereoisomer. Reagent choice matters: sodium borohydride usually reduces aldehydes and ketones but not esters, while lithium aluminium hydride reduces esters too. If no selective reagent exists, protect the interfering group. For example, to add a Grignard (organomagnesium) reagent to an alcohol-containing ketone, protect the alcohol as a silyl ether first, then remove it with fluoride.

sections.heading: Multi-step design
sections.text:
Multi-step design chooses an order that maximises overall yield and minimises steps, protecting groups and purification. Linear routes add one step at a time; convergent routes make fragments separately and join them late, which usually saves time and raises yield. Overall yield is the product of step yields.

Example: five steps, each 80%:
0.8⁵ = 0.32768, so overall yield is about 33%.
Check each step and revise the plan when a step fails.

keyPoints: Retrosynthesis works backwards from the target using disconnections and synthons.
Functional group interconversion changes a group to enable a planned reaction.
A protecting group must be easy to add, stable during the route, and easy to remove.
Orthogonal protecting groups are removed by independent conditions, such as Boc by acid and Fmoc by base.
Chemoselectivity controls which functional group reacts; protect when no selective reagent exists.
Overall yield is the product of step yields, so long linear routes lose material quickly.

en.title: Quantum chemistry and statistical mechanics
en.short: Schrödinger equation, approximation methods, molecular orbitals, partition functions and statistical thermodynamics.

sections.heading: Schrödinger equation
sections.text:
The time-independent Schrödinger equation is Ĥψ = Eψ. Ĥ is the Hamiltonian operator, ψ the wavefunction and E an allowed energy. For a particle in a one-dimensional box of length L, ψ_n = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L) and E_n = n²h² ÷ (8mL²).

Example: an electron in L = 1.00 nm has E₁ = (6.626 × 10⁻³⁴)² ÷ (8 × 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ × (1.00 × 10⁻⁹)²) = 6.02 × 10⁻²⁰ J, about 0.376 eV. Confinement raises the spacing between levels.

sections.heading: Approximation methods
sections.text: Exact solutions are rare. The variational method guesses a trial wavefunction and minimises the expectation value ⟨E⟩ = ∫ψ*Ĥψ dτ ÷ ∫ψ*ψ dτ; the lowest value is an upper bound to the true ground-state energy. Perturbation theory writes Ĥ = Ĥ⁰ + λV and expands energies and wavefunctions in powers of λ. It works well when V is small compared with Ĥ⁰. Both methods are used for atoms and molecules.

sections.heading: Molecular orbitals
sections.text: Molecular orbital (MO) theory combines atomic orbitals into MOs spread over the molecule. In the linear combination of atomic orbitals (LCAO) approach, ψ = Σ c_i φ_i. The coefficients and energies follow from the secular equations. Bonding MOs have lower energy and more electron density between nuclei; antibonding MOs have a node and higher energy. Filling MOs by the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion and Hund’s rules gives bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2. This explains H₂, O₂ and many spectra.

sections.heading: Statistical thermodynamics
sections.text: The Boltzmann distribution gives the probability of occupying energy level i: p_i = g_i exp(−E_i/kT) ÷ q, where q = Σ g_i exp(−E_i/kT) is the molecular partition function, g_i the degeneracy, k the Boltzmann constant and T temperature. For N independent indistinguishable molecules, the canonical partition function is Q = q^N ÷ N!. Thermodynamic functions follow from Q: U = kT²(∂ ln Q/∂T)_V and S = k ln Q + U/T. A larger q means more accessible states and greater entropy.

keyPoints: The time-independent Schrödinger equation is Ĥψ = Eψ; for a particle in a one-dimensional box, E_n = n²h² ÷ (8mL²).
The variational method gives an upper bound to the ground-state energy, while perturbation theory expands in a small perturbation.
In LCAO molecular orbital theory, bond order = (bonding electrons − antibonding electrons) ÷ 2.
The Boltzmann distribution is p_i = g_i exp(−E_i/kT) ÷ q, with molecular partition function q = Σ g_i exp(−E_i/kT).
For N indistinguishable molecules, the canonical partition function is Q = q^N ÷ N!.
Statistical thermodynamics gives U = kT²(∂ ln Q/∂T)_V and S = k ln Q + U/T; larger q means more accessible states and greater entropy.

en.title: Materials chemistry and nanochemistry
en.short: How nanomaterials are made and measured, why size changes properties, and where they are used.

sections.heading: Synthesis routes
sections.text: Nanomaterials have at least one dimension commonly between 1 and 100 nm. Top-down methods carve large solids down: ball milling and lithography. Bottom-up methods build from atoms or molecules: sol-gel processing, precipitation, chemical vapour deposition and colloidal synthesis. Bottom-up routes usually give better control of size and shape. In colloidal synthesis, precursor chemicals react in a solvent and capping ligands (molecules that bind the surface) stop the particles growing too large and keep them dispersed. The choice of route controls size distribution, purity and cost.

sections.heading: Characterisation
sections.text: X-ray diffraction (XRD) identifies crystal phases; the Scherrer equation, D = Kλ ÷ (β cos θ), estimates crystallite size D from peak broadening β. Electron microscopy (TEM and SEM) images size and shape directly. Dynamic light scattering (DLS) gives the hydrodynamic size in suspension. BET analysis measures specific surface area from gas adsorption. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) gives surface composition. UV-visible spectroscopy shows optical absorption, including plasmon bands. No single method is enough; results are cross-checked.

sections.heading: Size and surfaces
sections.text: As a particle shrinks, the surface area to volume ratio rises. For a cube of side L, ratio = 6L² ÷ L³ = 6 ÷ L. A 1,000 nm cube has 0.006 per nm; a 10 nm cube has 0.6 per nm, one hundred times larger. Surface atoms are less bonded, so surface energy is high and particles may aggregate. Capping ligands or charge (zeta potential) stabilise them. Size also changes electronic structure: quantum confinement widens the band gap of semiconductor nanocrystals, metal nanoparticles show surface plasmon resonance, and magnetic particles become superparamagnetic below a critical size.

sections.heading: Applications
sections.text: Materials chemistry uses these effects in catalysis (more surface sites per gram), sensors, drug delivery (nanoparticles carry drugs and release them), energy storage and conversion, and protective coatings. The same high surface area that makes a catalyst active can make a nanoparticle toxic or unstable, so applications need careful testing.

keyPoints: Nanomaterials have at least one dimension commonly between 1 and 100 nm, and their properties differ from the bulk material.
Top-down synthesis removes material; bottom-up synthesis builds from atoms or molecules and usually gives better size control.
The Scherrer equation D = Kλ ÷ (β cos θ) estimates crystallite size from XRD peak broadening.
For a cube of side L, surface area to volume ratio = 6 ÷ L, so smaller particles have much more surface.
Quantum confinement, surface plasmon resonance and superparamagnetism are size-dependent effects.
High surface energy causes aggregation; capping ligands or surface charge stabilise nanoparticles.

en.title: Research methods and dissertation in chemistry
en.short: Literature review, experimental design, uncertainty, ethics and writing a chemistry dissertation.

sections.heading: Literature review
sections.text: A literature review is an argument, not a list. It shows what is known, what is disputed and which gap your project fills. Search Scopus, Web of Science, SciFinder or Google Scholar, then follow citations forward and backward from key papers. Read the abstract, then the figures, then the methods. Ask whether the method was sound and whether the conclusions follow. Record every source in a reference manager as you read.

sections.heading: Experimental design
sections.text: Begin with a question your equipment can answer. Name the independent variable you change, the dependent variable you measure and the controls you hold constant. Include blanks, calibration standards and certified reference materials to separate signal from background. Run triplicates to estimate random error, and randomise run order so drift does not bias one sample. A pilot study is cheap insurance. Factorial designs vary several factors at once and expose interactions.

sections.heading: Data analysis and uncertainty
sections.text:
Random error scatters and shrinks when you average; systematic error is bias, and averaging will not remove it. Report a result as value ± expanded uncertainty, usually with coverage factor k = 2 for roughly 95% confidence, combining independent contributions in quadrature.

Example: 0.5000 g of solid (u = 0.0002 g) is dissolved and made to 250.0 mL (u = 0.12 mL).
c = 0.5000 ÷ 0.2500 = 2.000 g/L
relative u = √(0.0004² + 0.00048²) = 6.25 × 10⁻⁴
u(c) = 2.000 × 6.25 × 10⁻⁴ = 0.0013 g/L
Report 2.000 ± 0.003 g/L (k = 2).

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Never fabricate, falsify, plagiarise or selectively delete data. Keep a dated notebook and back up raw files. Agree authorship early; gift and ghost authorship are misconduct. Obtain ethics approval before work on humans or animals, and follow local rules for chemical waste. Structure the dissertation as abstract, introduction, literature review, methods, results, discussion, conclusion, references. Write methods and results while the work is fresh, and leave time for your supervisor to read drafts.

keyPoints: A literature review makes an argument about the gap your work fills; it is not a list of papers.
Define independent and dependent variables, controls, blanks and replicates before collecting data.
Random error falls with averaging; systematic error does not, so find and correct the bias.
Combine independent standard uncertainties in quadrature and report value ± expanded uncertainty with k = 2.
Fabrication, falsification, plagiarism and improper authorship are research misconduct.
Plan the dissertation chapters early and write methods and results while the work is fresh.
